trial_name: ARMA — Ventilation with Lower Tidal Volumes vs Traditional Tidal Volumes in ALI/ARDS (2000)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network. Ventilation with lower tidal volumes as compared with traditional tidal volumes for acute lung injury and the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(18):1301-1308.
one_liner: Lower tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤30 cm H2O) reduced mortality and increased ventilator-free days in ALI/ARDS compared with traditional tidal volumes.

pico.population: Adults with ALI/ARDS requiring invasive mechanical ventilation
pico.intervention: Lung-protective ventilation: initial tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW), plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O, FiO2/PEEP table guidance, permissive hypercapnia within protocolised pH thresholds
pico.comparison: Traditional ventilation: initial tidal volume 12 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤50 cm H2O, same gas-exchange targets and weaning protocol
pico.outcome: Primary: death before discharge home with unassisted breathing. Key secondary: ventilator-free days to day 28, days without nonpulmonary organ failure, mortality at day 180

background.existing_knowledge: By the mid-1990s, ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma/barotrauma and biotrauma) was increasingly recognised as an iatrogenic amplifier of acute lung injury. Common practice used large tidal volumes (10–15 mL/kg) with permissive plateau pressures exceeding what is now considered safe. Small randomised trials of protective strategies produced conflicting results, and a definitive trial was needed.
background.knowledge_gap: Small randomised trials of protective strategies produced conflicting results, and a definitive, adequately powered multicentre trial was needed.
background.hypothesis: In intubated adults with ALI/ARDS, a ventilation strategy targeting lower tidal volumes and lower plateau pressures reduces mortality and increases ventilator-free days compared with traditional tidal volumes.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, parallel-group, investigator-initiated ARDS Network trial in 10 university-affiliated centres (United States).
methods.setting: ICUs at 10 university-affiliated centres in the United States.

inclusion: Bilateral infiltrates consistent with pulmonary oedema
No clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension (pulmonary-artery wedge pressure ≤18 mm Hg if measured)
exclusion: Weight >1 kg per cm of height

methods.intervention: Initial tidal volume 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O; adjustments permitted 4–8 mL/kg depending on plateau pressure and pH. Gas-exchange targets: PaO2 55–80 mmHg or SpO2 88–95% using protocolised FiO2/PEEP table. Increased respiratory rate to offset reduced tidal volume; permissive hypercapnia allowed within protocolised pH thresholds. Daily weaning assessment.
methods.comparison: Initial tidal volume 12 mL/kg PBW with plateau pressure limit ≤50 cm H2O; same gas-exchange targets, FiO2/PEEP table, and weaning protocol as intervention.
methods.blinding: Open-label; unblinded to clinicians and investigators.
methods.sample_size_power: Original power calculation not reported; trial stopped early at fourth interim analysis per group sequential design.
methods.primary_outcome: Death before discharge home with unassisted breathing.
secondary_outcomes: Ventilator-free days (days alive and breathing without assistance to day 28)
Days without failure of any nonpulmonary organ system to day 28
Barotrauma (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, pneumoperitoneum, subcutaneous emphysema, or air cysts)
methods.follow_up: Daily through day 28; survival and breathing status assessed to day 180.

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early at fourth interim analysis: lower tidal volume group had significantly lower mortality (P=0.005 at interim, stopping boundary 0.023).
Primary outcome (death before discharge home with unassisted breathing): 31.0% vs 39.8%, absolute difference 8.8 percentage points (95% CI 2.4–15.3, P=0.007).
Ventilator-free days to day 28 were higher (12±11 vs 10±11 days, P=0.007), and mortality benefit persisted at 180 days (34.7% vs 42.5%, P=0.007).
Barotrauma was not significantly different (10% vs 11%, P=0.43).

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary composite (death before discharge home with unassisted breathing)

outcomes_table.note: Mean ± SD reported; CI not provided

outcomes_table.outcome: Days without nonpulmonary organ failure (to day 28)

safety: Barotrauma occurred in 10% (43/432) in the lower tidal volume group vs 11% (47/429) in the traditional group (P=0.43); no excess barotrauma observed.

Physiological changes: higher PaCO2 (44 ± 11 vs 40 ± 10 mm Hg) and lower pH (7.38 ± 0.07 vs 7.41 ± 0.07) on day 1, consistent with permissive hypercapnia. No reported safety concerns from these changes.

domains.notes: Central randomisation via automated telephone system; concealed allocation; factorial co-randomisation to ketoconazole/lisofylline balanced by design.
Open-label; primary outcomes are objective (mortality, ventilator-free days) reducing assessment bias, but potential for differential co-interventions (e.g., PEEP differences).
ITT analysis; 180-day vital status missing for 9 patients (1% missing); primary in-hospital outcomes were essentially complete.
Substantial separation in tidal volume (6.2 vs 11.8 mL/kg PBW) and plateau pressure (25 vs 33 cm H2O). Small but significant PEEP difference (8.3 vs 7.3 cm H2O on day 1, P<0.001).
Groups well matched: age 51±17 vs 52±18 years; APACHE III 81±28 vs 84±28; PaO2/FiO2 138±64 vs 134±58; baseline plateau pressure 33±10 vs 33±11 cm H2O.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity moderate-to-strong: randomised, concealed allocation, objective outcomes, clear protocol separation, but open-label and small PEEP difference; early stopping may overestimate effect size.

domains.notes: Typical adult ALI/ARDS case-mix (baseline PaO2/FiO2 ~135–140; plateau pressure ~33 cm H2O) but excludes important subgroups: severe chronic respiratory disease, intracranial hypertension, extreme obesity, major burns, high competing mortality.

Feasible in most ventilated ICU settings; requires accurate height measurement, PBW calculation, staff training in permissive hypercapnia and plateau pressure monitoring. Low-cost intervention but may need adequate monitoring capacity.

external_validity.verdict: Findings are highly generalisable to adult ALI/ARDS patients in well-resourced ICUs, but should be extrapolated cautiously to excluded groups and to contexts with limited monitoring/training.

strengths: Large, multicentre randomised trial with central allocation concealment within an established critical care network.
Clear, protocolised ventilator management with large, quantifiable separation in tidal volume and plateau pressure.
Clinically meaningful, objective primary outcomes with follow-up to 180 days.
Consistent directionality across mortality and ventilator/organ-failure–free outcomes.
limitations: Unblinded intervention with potential for differential co-interventions (including small but significant PEEP differences early after randomisation).
Early stopping for benefit increases the risk of overestimating effect size and limits precision.
Control strategy (12 mL/kg PBW; plateau pressure limit ≤50) may be viewed as injurious by contemporary standards, complicating interpretation as optimisation vs harm avoidance.
Power calculation and original target sample size not reported, limiting transparency around planned operating characteristics.

critical_appraisal.summary: ARMA provides robust evidence that a lung-protective strategy (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤30 cm H2O) improves survival and organ function in ALI/ARDS, though the open-label design, early stopping, and control-arm issues warrant some caution.
weaknesses: Control arm not reflective of current practice

sections.authors_conclusion: In adults with ALI/ARDS, ventilation with lower tidal volumes (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O) reduced mortality and increased ventilator-free days compared with traditional tidal volumes.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Lower tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤30 cm H2O) is now standard of care for ARDS; this trial showed a significant mortality benefit.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with ALI/ARDS who are invasively ventilated in well-resourced ICUs, excluding those with severe chronic respiratory disease, intracranial hypertension, or extreme obesity.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean that all patients require exactly 6 mL/kg; rather, a range of 4–8 mL/kg guided by plateau pressure and pH is acceptable. Not a mandate for universal permissive hypercapnia without safe limits.
implementation_caveats: Accurate height measurement and PBW calculation essential.
Staff education on managing permissive hypercapnia safely.
Potential need for increased sedation in some patients.

controversies.notes: The comparison was between bundled ventilation strategies including slightly higher PEEP in the lower tidal volume group, raising uncertainty about which component mediated the benefit.
The traditional tidal volume arm (12 mL/kg, plateau ≤50) may be injurious; the trial thus demonstrates harm avoidance rather than an optimal target.
Early termination for benefit may overestimate effect size, though conservative stopping boundaries and 180-day mortality results support the conclusion.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal tidal volume (e.g., 4 vs 6 vs 8 mL/kg)?
Is higher PEEP with lower tidal volumes beneficial beyond ARMA's protocol?
How to best implement lung-protective ventilation in resource-limited settings?
Is there a role for even lower tidal volumes in severe ARDS?
Does the benefit extend to non-ARDS patients?

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: 31.0% vs 39.8% mortality, absolute reduction 8.8% (95% CI 2.4–15.3)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ARDS, ventilating with 6 mL/kg predicted body weight and limiting plateau pressure to ≤30 cm H2O saves lives compared to traditional 12 mL/kg strategy.
